definition: The branch of chemistry dealing with the compounds of carbon. Also called the chemistry of carbon compounds.
The key atom of carbon compounds. A carbon atom can form four bonds and can therefore be linked into chains, branches and rings – the reason there are millions of carbon compounds.
A diagram showing how the atoms in a molecule are bonded to each other. Each carbon atom is drawn with its four bonds ("arms").
A form of pure carbon in which each carbon atom is tightly bonded to four others in all directions. The hardest substance known – used in jewellery and cutting tools.
A form of pure carbon in which the carbon atoms lie in flat layers that slide against each other. Soft and rubs off – used in pencil leads and as a lubricant.
A form of pure carbon in which the carbon atoms form ball-shaped molecules resembling a football. Discovered in the 1980s–90s and very stable.
Extremely porous carbon with an enormous surface area that can absorb colour, odour, taste and toxic substances. Found in kitchen extractor fans, gas masks, and used as a medicine for poisoning.
A carbon compound that contains only carbon and hydrogen. Most fuels are hydrocarbons.

A saturated hydrocarbon in the methane series, with only single bonds. Follows the formula CnH2n+2. The first ten are methane, ethane, propane, butane, pentane, hexane, heptane, octane, nonane and decane.
A hydrocarbon in which the carbon atoms have only single bonds and bond to as many hydrogen atoms as possible. Alkanes are saturated.
The series of alkanes that starts with methane, in which each next substance has one more carbon atom: methane, ethane, propane, butane, and so on.
A hydrocarbon that contains a double or triple bond between carbon atoms. Alkenes and alkynes are unsaturated.
An unsaturated hydrocarbon with a double bond between two carbon atoms. The simplest is ethene (C2H4), a raw material for plastics.
An unsaturated hydrocarbon with a triple bond between two carbon atoms. The simplest is ethyne (C2H2), also called acetylene, which is used in welding.
A carbon compound in which a hydrogen atom has been replaced by an −OH group. Named with the ending -ol. Methanol and ethanol are the simplest.
A hydroxyl group (one oxygen atom and one hydrogen atom, −OH). It is the OH group that makes a substance an alcohol.
The alcohol found in wine and spirits (C2H5OH). Formed when yeast converts sugar. Also used as a solvent and as a fuel.
The simplest alcohol (CH3OH), also called wood alcohol. Highly toxic – small amounts can cause blindness or death. Must never be confused with ethanol.
An alcohol with several OH groups. Two OH groups make a dihydric alcohol (glycol), three make a trihydric one (glycerol).
A dihydric alcohol (two OH groups). Lowers the freezing point and is used as antifreeze in car radiators. Toxic.
A trihydric alcohol (three OH groups), also called glycerine. Harmless, sweet and moisture-retaining – found in skin cream and food, and forms part of fats.
A carbon compound with a carboxyl group (−COOH) that makes the solution acidic. Named with the ending -oic acid. Examples: formic acid and acetic acid.
The atomic group −COOH that characterises an organic acid. It can release a hydrogen ion, which is why it makes the solution acidic.
An organic acid (ethanoic acid, CH3COOH) that gives vinegar its sour taste. Vinegar is diluted acetic acid.
A substance formed when an alcohol reacts with an organic acid, releasing water at the same time. Many esters smell of fruit; fats are esters.
The reaction in which an alcohol and an organic acid form an ester and water.
An organic acid in which a hydrogen atom has been replaced by an amino group (−NH2). Has both a carboxyl group and an amino group. Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins.
The atomic group −NH2 (a nitrogen-containing group) which, together with the carboxyl group, characterises an amino acid.
